title: Google Rolls Out Gemini 4 Hydrogen to Search and Opens Preorders for Gemini Smart Glasses
excerpt: Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Nov. 12, putting the faster AI model into Search worldwide, and opened preorders for Gemini smart glasses from $395.
content:
Google released a new artificial intelligence model, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, on Nov. 12 — and put it straight into Google Search for users worldwide, in what the company calls its largest model upgrade to Search so far.

Hydrogen is the fast, lower-cost member of Google's Gemini 4 family and the successor to Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google says it completes tasks 2.5 times faster than 3.8 Flash, and it scored 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default reasoning level — one point higher than the larger Gemini 4 Argon model, according to reports on the launch.

For developers, the pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, across a 1 million-token context window. The model is generally available through Google's Gemini API, and it is also rolling out in the Gemini app, in Google's Antigravity coding platform and in tools including Cursor and Devin, according to coverage of Google's announcement.

Search changes first

The most immediate change for most people is in Google Search, which now runs on Gemini 4 Hydrogen for all users worldwide. Google says the model helps Search handle complicated questions and typos better. Readers in Laredo may notice answers in Search becoming faster or more detailed — the same model now sits behind the search box millions of people here use every day.

Smart glasses open for preorder

On the same day, Google opened preorders for its first Intelligent Eyewear — smart glasses powered by Gemini, developed with Samsung and eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Sales begin Dec. 10.

Warby Parker offers three frames starting at $395 in the United States, and Gentle Monster offers six styles starting at $449 in the United States and South Korea. The glasses have no display. They pair a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera, open-ear speakers and microphones with Gemini, weigh about 41 grams and last up to nine hours per charge, according to Google's announcement as reported this week.

Wearers can ask Gemini about what they are looking at, get walking directions or translate conversations, according to Google. The glasses include privacy measures such as a tamper-proof LED indicator that lights up when the camera is recording.

Questions to watch

As with every wave of AI-powered hardware, the launch raises questions that matter beyond Silicon Valley: what the glasses' cameras mean for privacy in public places, how much of daily life gets routed through one company's AI, and whether the technology stays affordable or becomes another premium gadget. Google has not announced a Laredo retail date; preorders are available online and in stores through both eyewear brands.
